claim: RBM47 was identified as a suppressor of breast cancer progression and metastasis through integrative analysis of clinical breast cancer gene expression datasets, cell line models, and mutation data from cancer genome resequencing studies.
source: Through integrative analysis of clinical breast cancer gene expression datasets, cell line models of breast cancer progression, and mutation data from cancer genome resequencing studies, we identified RNA binding motif protein 47 (RBM47) as a suppressor of breast cancer progression and metastasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental approach described in the abstract and detailed in the results section, combining multiple data sources.

claim: RBM47 inhibited breast cancer re-initiation and growth in experimental models.
source: RBM47 inhibited breast cancer re-initiation and growth in experimental models.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo models shown in the manuscript.

claim: Transcriptome-wide HITS-CLIP analysis revealed widespread RBM47 binding to mRNAs, most prominently in introns and 3′UTRs.
source: Transcriptome-wide HITS-CLIP analysis revealed widespread RBM47 binding to mRNAs, most prominently in introns and 3′UTRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by HITS-CLIP experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: RBM47 altered splicing and abundance of a subset of its target mRNAs.
source: RBM47 altered splicing and abundance of a subset of its target mRNAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq and HITS-CLIP data showing changes in mRNA levels and splicing patterns.

claim: Dickkopf WNT signaling pathway inhibitor 1 (DKK1) is stabilized by RBM47 and inhibits tumor progression downstream of RBM47.
source: Some of the mRNAs stabilized by RBM47, as exemplified by dickkopf WNT signaling pathway inhibitor 1, inhibit tumor progression downstream of RBM47.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing DKK1 mRNA stabilization and functional assays.

claim: RBM47 was the only gene that fulfilled the criteria of reduced mRNA expression in functionally metastatic cancer cells, low mRNA expression associated with poor patient outcome, and enriched mutation in a brain metastasis.
source: RBM47, a gene encoding a previously uncharacterized putative RNA-binding protein was the only one that fulfilled all these criteria (Baltz et al., 2012; Castello et al., 2012; Ray et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by the integrative analysis of multiple datasets as described in the methods.

claim: RBM47 mRNA expression is lower in highly metastatic cells compared to parental cells.
source: We confirmed the lower expression of RBM47 mRNA in the highly metastatic cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Lower RBM47 mRNA expression translates into a comparable difference at the protein level.
source: This translated into a comparable difference at the protein level (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Low RBM47 mRNA expression is significantly associated with relapse to brain and lung in clinical datasets.
source: In the clinical data sets, low RBM47 mRNA expression was significantly associated with relapse to brain and lung (Figure 1D,E) but not to bone (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis of clinical data shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: Low RBM47 mRNA expression is not significantly associated with relapse to bone in clinical datasets.
source: In the clinical data sets, low RBM47 mRNA expression was significantly associated with relapse to brain and lung (Figure 1D,E) but not to bone (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis of clinical data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: In multivariate analysis combining RBM47 expression with ER, PR and HER2 receptor status, the association with brain metastasis remained statistically significant.
source: In multivariate analysis combining RBM47 expression with estrogen, progesterone and HER2 receptor status (ER, PR and HER2), the association with brain metastasis remained statistically significant (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by multivariate Cox proportional hazards model analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Low RBM47 expression is significantly associated with claudin-low and basal breast cancers in the TCGA cohort.
source: We found that low RBM47 expression was significantly associated with claudin-low and basal breast cancers (Figure 1G), two subtypes of poor prognosis (Smid et al., 2008; Lu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data from the TCGA cohort shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Claudin-low and basal breast cancers are two subtypes of poor prognosis.
source: We found that low RBM47 expression was significantly associated with claudin-low and basal breast cancers (Figure 1G), two subtypes of poor prognosis (Smid et al., 2008; Lu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The RBM47I281fs mutation truncates the protein from the third RNA recognition motif (RRM) onwards.
source: The RBM47I281fs mutation first reported in a brain metastasis truncates the protein from the third RNA recognition motif (RRM) onwards (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by the protein structure diagram shown in Figure 1H and reference to the mutation.

claim: The RBM47I281fs mutation was already present in a minority subpopulation of the corresponding primary tumor.
source: As this mutation was already present in a minority subpopulation of the corresponding primary tumor (Ding et al., 2010), we looked for additional evidence of genetic RBM47 aberrations in primary breast cancer cohorts.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ding et al., 2010.

claim: The COSMIC database reported 9 non-synonymous mutations in RBM47, three of which were frameshift mutations truncating one or more of the RRM domains.
source: The catalogue of somatic mutations in cancer (COSMIC) database (Forbes et al., 2010) reported 9 non-synonymous mutations in RBM47, three of which were frameshift mutations truncating one or more of the RRM domains (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the COSMIC database shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In basal breast cancer, RBM47 was targeted by a mutation or homozygous deletion in approximately 8% of the cases in the TCGA cohort.
source: Furthermore, analysis of the data from the TCGA cohort revealed that in basal breast cancer, RBM47 was targeted by a mutation or homozygous deletion in ∼8% of the cases (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Heterozygous loss of the RBM47 locus was present in 30% of the TCGA cohort.
source: Moreover, heterozygous loss of the RBM47 locus was present in 30% of the TCGA cohort (Cerami et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of TCGA data with citation to Cerami et al., 2012.

claim: Wild type RBM47 inhibited lung colonization by MDA231-LM2 cells when compared to RBM47I281fs.
source: As determined by in vivo bioluminescence in experimental metastasis assays, wild type RBM47 inhibited lung colonization by the MDA231-LM2 cells, when compared to RBM47I281fs (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo bioluminescence data shown in Figures 2A-B.

claim: Wild type RBM47 extended brain metastasis free survival in mice inoculated with MDA231-BrM2 cells when compared to RBM47I281fs.
source: Similarly, we observed extended brain metastasis free survival in mice inoculated with the MDA231-BrM2 cells expressing RBM47 when compared to those expressing RBM47I281fs (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The difference in brain metastasis free survival translated into reduced brain metastatic burden as determined by ex vivo imaging.
source: This difference translated into reduced brain metastatic burden as determined by ex vivo imaging (Figure 2D,E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo bioluminescence imaging data shown in Figures 2D, 2E, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Two RBM47-targeting shRNA constructs significantly shortened the lung metastasis free survival in mice when compared to controls.
source: Two RBM47-targeting shRNA constructs significantly shortened the lung metastasis free survival in mice when compared to controls (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), as determined by bioluminescence imaging (Figure 2G,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis and bioluminescence imaging data shown in Figures 2F-H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Despite robust mRNA expression, the mutant RBM47I281fs protein levels were low, indicating that the mutant protein was unstable and therefore inactive.
source: Of note, despite robust mRNA expression, the mutant RBM47I281fs protein levels were low, indicating that the mutant protein was unstable and therefore inactive (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Some cancer clones were able to form robust lung metastasis even in the presence of RBM47.
source: This revealed that some cancer clones were able to form robust lung metastasis even in the presence of RBM47 (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), but that many of the metastases formed after the inoculation of wild type RBM47-expressing cells had avoided or suppressed the expression of RBM47 (Figure 3B, Figure 3A—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Many of the metastases formed after the inoculation of wild type RBM47-expressing cells had avoided or suppressed the expression of RBM47.
source: This revealed that some cancer clones were able to form robust lung metastasis even in the presence of RBM47 (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), but that many of the metastases formed after the inoculation of wild type RBM47-expressing cells had avoided or suppressed the expression of RBM47 (Figure 3B, Figure 3A—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The rate of proliferation as determined by Ki67 immunohistochemistry did not correlate with the level of RBM47 expression.
source: The rate of proliferation as determined by Ki67 immunohistochemistry did not correlate with the level of RBM47 expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Ki67 immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The induction of RBM47 expression with doxycycline inhibited robustly brain colonization of both metastatic cell clones, WT6 and WT10.
source: The induction of RBM47 expression with doxycycline in the diet inhibited robustly brain colonization of both metastatic cell clones, WT6 and WT10 (Figure 3E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo and ex vivo bioluminescence data shown in Figures 3E-G.

claim: The patient-derived mutant RBM47I281fs did not show any tumor suppressive effects.
source: However, the patient-derived mutant RBM47I281fs did not show any tumor suppressive effects (Figure 3H–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo and ex vivo bioluminescence data shown in Figures 3H-J.

claim: RBM47 can directly bind RNA in vivo.
source: To determine whether RBM47 can directly bind RNA in vivo, we made use of the ability of UV-irradiation at 254 nm to induce chemical crosslinks between RNA and proteins that are in direct contact (Darnell, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by UV-crosslinking experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: γ-32P-labeled RNA was detected by autoradiogram at approximately 76 kD, the predicted size of Flag-RBM47, in Flag-immunoprecipitates from UV-irradiated, doxycycline-treated MDA231-BrM2 WT Flag-RBM47 cells.
source: γ-32P-labeled RNA was detected by autoradiogram at ∼76 kD, the predicted size of Flag-RBM47, in Flag-immunoprecipitates from UV-irradiated, doxycycline-treated MDA231-BrM2 WT Flag-RBM47 cells, but not doxycycline-treated empty vector control or non-irradiated WT Flag-RBM47 expressing cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by autoradiogram data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: RBM47 HITS-CLIP yielded approximately 7.7 × 10^6 and approximately 2.0 × 10^6 unique reads (tags) per replicate.
source: RBM47-bound HITS-CLIP reads were mapped to the human genome, yielding ∼7.7 × 106 and ∼2.0 × 106 unique reads (tags) per replicate.
evidence: This claim is supported by HITS-CLIP sequencing data.

claim: 75% of the HITS-CLIP tags mapped to regions corresponding to UCSC/Refseq genes.
source: 75% of the tags mapped to regions corresponding to UCSC/Refseq genes, with a high degree of reproducibility of binding observed between replicates (Spearmann correlation coefficient R2 = 0.998, total tags per gene, Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by HITS-CLIP data analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There is a high degree of reproducibility of RBM47 binding observed between replicates (Spearmann correlation coefficient R2 = 0.998).
source: 75% of the tags mapped to regions corresponding to UCSC/Refseq genes, with a high degree of reproducibility of binding observed between replicates (Spearmann correlation coefficient R2 = 0.998, total tags per gene, Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of HITS-CLIP data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Increasing the stringency of biologically reproducible RBM47 binding site definition reveals predominant binding in 3′UTRs and intronic regions of target transcripts.
source: Increasing the stringency of biologically reproducible RBM47 binding site definition reveals predominant binding in 3′UTRs and intronic regions of target transcripts, with the most robust binding (tags per binding site) evident in 3′UTRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by HITS-CLIP data analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: MEME analysis reveals an enrichment for polyU sequences in the ±10 nt footprint region surrounding reproducible RBM47 deletion CIMS.
source: MEME analysis reveals an enrichment for polyU sequences (50 sites, p=2.4e−16) in the ±10 nt foot print region surrounding reproducible RBM47 deletion CIMS (357 sites with ≥5 mutations, FDR ≤0.01, Zhang and Darnell, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by MEME motif analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Widespread RBM47 binding is seen in target transcripts, as exemplified by binding patterns seen in the 3′UTRs of DKK1 and IL8.
source: Widespread RBM47 binding is seen in target transcripts, as exemplified by binding patterns seen in the 3′UTRs of DKK1 and IL8.
evidence: This claim is supported by HITS-CLIP data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: RNA-seq analysis revealed 121 and 140 CA exons with significant RBM47-dependent inclusion and exclusion, respectively.
source: This analysis revealed 121 and 140 CA exons with significant RBM47-dependent inclusion and exclusion, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Forty-eight RBM47-bound included and 49 RBM47-bound excluded CA exons were identified in a total of 84 genes.
source: Forty-eight RBM47-bound included and 49 RBM47-bound excluded CA exons were identified in a total of 84 genes (Figure 5B; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by combined HITS-CLIP and RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: RBM47-dependent splicing changes were confirmed via RT-PCR for SLK, MDM4, LIMCH1, MBNL1 and SEC31A.
source: RBM47-dependent splicing changes were confirmed via RT-PCR as shown for SLK, MDM4, LIMCH1, MBNL1 and SEC31A (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR validation data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The normalized complexity map reveals enriched RBM47 binding in the vicinity of splice acceptor sites of the CA exon and 3′ CE for included alternative isoforms.
source: The resulting normalized complexity map reveals enriched RBM47 binding in the vicinity of splice acceptor sites of the CA exon and 3′ CE for included alternative isoforms, while relative enrichment of RBM47 binding was seen at the 5′ CE splice donor and 3′CE splice acceptor of excluded isoforms.
evidence: This claim is supported by the normalized complexity map shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Relative enrichment of RBM47 binding was seen at the 5′ CE splice donor and 3′CE splice acceptor of excluded isoforms.
source: The resulting normalized complexity map reveals enriched RBM47 binding in the vicinity of splice acceptor sites of the CA exon and 3′ CE for included alternative isoforms, while relative enrichment of RBM47 binding was seen at the 5′ CE splice donor and 3′CE splice acceptor of excluded isoforms.
evidence: This claim is supported by the normalized complexity map shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The mRNA level of several more genes correlated significantly with increasing concentrations of doxycycline in both cell lines expressing the wild type RBM47 (WT6 and WT10), when compared to cells expressing the mutant.
source: First, genome-wide analyses showed that the mRNA level of several more genes correlated significantly with increasing concentrations of doxycycline in both cell lines expressing the wild type RBM47 (WT6 and WT10), when compared to cells expressing the mutant (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A set of 102 mRNAs were upregulated and 92 were downregulated in cells expressing the wild type RBM47.
source: This revealed a set of 102 mRNAs that were upregulated and 92 that were downregulated, respectively, in cells expressing the wild type RBM47 (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: These changes in mRNA levels were observed already with the lowest expression level of RBM47 that was comparable or lower than those detected in endogenously RBM47 expressing cells.
source: Importantly, these changes were observed already with the lowest expression level of RBM47 that was comparable or lower than those detected in endogenously RBM47 expressing cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of RBM47 expression levels shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D,E.

claim: Unsupervised hierarchical clustering analysis of the TCGA cohort using the 194 RBM47-responsive genes revealed two main clusters, one of which harbored characteristics of the RBM47-low phenotype.
source: To determine whether the 194 RBM47-responsive genes displayed clinically meaningful expression patterns, we conducted an unsupervised hierarchical clustering analysis of the TCGA cohort of breast cancer specimens. Two main clusters emerged, one of which harbored characteristics of the RBM47-low phenotype ('Cluster 2', Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Cluster 2 had significantly lower RBM47 expression levels when compared to Cluster 1.
source: First, this subgroup, Cluster 2, had significantly lower RBM47 expression levels when compared to Cluster 1 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RBM47 expression analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The genes that were induced upon RBM47 reintroduction tended to have lower expression in Cluster 2, whereas genes with reduced expression level in the RBM47-expressing cells tended to show higher expression in Cluster 2.
source: Second, the genes that were induced upon RBM47 reintroduction tended to have lower expression in Cluster 2, whereas genes with reduced expression level in the RBM47-expressing cells tended to show higher expression in Cluster 2 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Of the 2498 strongest binding partners with >100 tags per transcript, 25 were among the 102 RBM47-upregulated genes and 17 among the 92 RBM47-downregulated genes.
source: Of the 2498 strongest binding partners with >100 tags per transcript (total tags in BC2 tags ≥10 clusters; Supplementary file 3), 25 were among the 102 RBM47-upregulated genes and 17 among the 92 RBM47-downregulated genes (Figure 6F), indicating no significant binding preference for either groups.
evidence: This claim is supported by combined HITS-CLIP and RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: IL8 and DKK1 were among the top-scoring RBM47 binding mRNAs and were among the upregulated genes.
source: Two of the top-scoring RBM47 binding mRNAs, IL8 and DKK1 (17,079 and 16,208 tags in clusters per gene, respectively, Figure 4G), were among the upregulated genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by HITS-CLIP and RNA-seq data shown in Figures 4G and 6G.

claim: The increase in DKK1 and IL8 mRNA levels was associated with increased protein secretion as determined by ELISA.
source: This increase in mRNA levels was associated with increased protein secretion as determined by ELISA, whereas VEGFA, the mRNA of which was bound but not upregulated by RBM47, showed no change in protein secretion (Figure 6H).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: VEGFA mRNA was bound but not upregulated by RBM47 and showed no change in protein secretion.
source: This increase in mRNA levels was associated with increased protein secretion as determined by ELISA, whereas VEGFA, the mRNA of which was bound but not upregulated by RBM47, showed no change in protein secretion (Figure 6H).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Knockdown of RBM47 in SKBR3 and ZR-75-30 cells reduced DKK1 mRNA levels.
source: As predicted by our results in WT6 and WT10 cells, knockdown of RBM47 in two additional breast cancer cell lines expressing high levels of endogenous RBM47, SKBR3 and ZR-75-30, reduced DKK1 mRNA levels (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Wild type RBM47, but not the RBM47I281fs mutant, was able to increase the half-life of DKK1 mRNA by up to fourfold.
source: This demonstrated that wild type RBM47, but not the RBM47I281fs mutant, was able to increase the half-life of DKK1 mRNA by up to fourfold (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by mRNA stability assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: RBM47 inhibited the capability of the 3′-targeting shRNA-miRs to keep the DKK1 mRNA level down.
source: In contrast, RBM47 inhibited the capability of the 3′-targeting shRNA-miRs to keep the DKK1 mRNA level down (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The induction of RBM47 expression did not have a significant effect on the efficiency of the 5′-targeting shRNA-miRs.
source: The induction of RBM47 expression did not have a significant effect on the efficiency on the 5′-targeting shRNA-miRs (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Doxycycline-induced expression of RBM47 in WT6 cells led to a dampened Wnt3A-dependent AXIN2 induction.
source: Doxycycline-induced expression of RBM47 in WT6 cells led to a dampened Wnt3A-dependent AXIN2 induction (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The inhibition of AXIN2 expression by RBM47 was at least partially dependent on DKK1.
source: This inhibition of AXIN2 expression was at least partially dependent on DKK1 (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data with DKK1 knockdown shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Human breast cancers with low RBM47 expression had in general higher levels of Wnt transcriptomic activity when compared to tumors with high RBM47 expression in the TCGA cohort.
source: In agreement with these results, human breast cancers with low RBM47 expression had in general higher levels of Wnt transcriptomic activity when compared to tumors with high RBM47 expression in the TCGA cohort (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Wnt pathway activity analysis in the TCGA cohort shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The induction of RBM47 by doxycycline was able to significantly delay the emergence of mammary tumors.
source: The induction of RBM47 by doxycycline was able to significantly delay the emergence of mammary tumors (Figure 8D), and the tumors that formed were smaller in size (Figure 8E).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo bioluminescence data shown in Figures 8D and 8E.

claim: Inhibition of DKK1 expression in the MDA231-BrM2 cells promoted tumor formation in the orthotopic site.
source: In line with this, inhibition of DKK1 expression in the MDA231-BrM2 cells promoted tumor formation in the orthotopic site (Figure 8F, Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo bioluminescence data shown in Figure 8F and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Only 1/9 mice (16%) injected with control cells developed brain metastasis, whereas 8/17 mice (47%) inoculated with DKK1 RNAi construct transduced cells developed metastasis.
source: Only 1/9 mice (16%) injected with control cells developed brain metastasis, whereas 8/17 mice (47%) inoculated with DKK1 RNAi construct transduced cells developed metastasis (Figure 8G,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo bioluminescence data shown in Figures 8G and 8H.

claim: RBM47 contains three classical RNA recognition motifs (RRM domains).
source: RBM47 contains three classical RNA recognition motifs (RRM domains).
evidence: This is a statement about the protein structure of RBM47.

claim: The closest homologs of RBM47 are Apobec1 complementation factor (A1CF) and hnRNP-Q.
source: The closest homologs of RBM47 are Apobec1 complementation factor (A1CF) and hnRNP-Q, which regulate RNA editing (Mehta et al., 2000) and splicing and transcript stability, respectively (Chen et al., 2008; Weidensdorfer et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence homology analysis and citations to published literature.

claim: A1CF regulates RNA editing.
source: The closest homologs of RBM47 are Apobec1 complementation factor (A1CF) and hnRNP-Q, which regulate RNA editing (Mehta et al., 2000) and splicing and transcript stability, respectively (Chen et al., 2008; Weidensdorfer et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mehta et al., 2000.

claim: hnRNP-Q regulates splicing and transcript stability.
source: The closest homologs of RBM47 are Apobec1 complementation factor (A1CF) and hnRNP-Q, which regulate RNA editing (Mehta et al., 2000) and splicing and transcript stability, respectively (Chen et al., 2008; Weidensdorfer et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2008 and Weidensdorfer et al., 2009.

claim: RBM47 binds robustly to approximately 2500 gene transcripts in human breast cancer cells.
source: We find that RBM47 binds robustly to ∼2500 gene transcripts in human breast cancer cells, with only a subset showing steady state level change or alternative splicing upon RBM47 reintroduction.
evidence: This claim is supported by HITS-CLIP data analysis.

claim: Only a subset of RBM47-bound transcripts show steady state level change or alternative splicing upon RBM47 reintroduction.
source: We find that RBM47 binds robustly to ∼2500 gene transcripts in human breast cancer cells, with only a subset showing steady state level change or alternative splicing upon RBM47 reintroduction.
evidence: This claim is supported by combined HITS-CLIP and RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: The RRM-domain containing protein HuR modulates the destabilizing effects of miRNAs and AUF1 on common target transcripts.
source: For example, the RRM-domain containing protein HuR modulates the destabilizing effects of miRNAs (Bhattacharyya et al., 2006; Kim et al., 2009; Young et al., 2012) and AUF1 (Zou et al., 2010) on common target transcripts.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: DKK1 is a secreted Wnt inhibitor.
source: One of the most highly bound RBM47 mRNA targets, the secreted Wnt inhibitor DKK1, is stabilized by RBM47 and partially mediates RBM47 tumor suppressive function.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DKK1 function.

claim: rbm47 knockdown in zebra fish embryos leads to a headless phenotype mediated via up-regulation of the wnt8a pathway.
source: Interestingly, rbm47 knockdown in zebra fish embryos leads to a headless phenotype mediated via up-regulation of the wnt8a pathway (Guan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Guan et al., 2013.

claim: Low-frequency cancer mutations can give rise to tumorigenic phenotypes.
source: First, we show that low-frequency cancer mutations can give rise to tumorigenic phenotypes.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the study of RBM47.

claim: Loss of a broadly targeted and multifunctional RBP can increase the fitness of certain cancer cell clones in support of metastasis.
source: Second, we show that loss of a broadly targeted and multifunctional RBP can increase the fitness of certain cancer cell clones in support of metastasis.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the study of RBM47.

claim: Deregulation of RNA-binding proteins is emerging as a prominent source of complex transcriptomic diversity that can serve as a platform for the selection of metastatic traits during tumor progression.
source: Deregulation of RNA-binding proteins is thus emerging as a prominent source of complex transcriptomic diversity that can serve as a platform for the selection of metastatic traits during tumor progression.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the study and broader literature context.

claim: Cancers arise through an evolutionary process that feeds from stochastic genetic alterations and selection.
source: Cancers arise through an evolutionary process that feeds from stochastic genetic alterations and selection (Vogelstein et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Vogelstein et al., 2013.

claim: Several independent studies have characterized the mutational complement of breast cancer.
source: For example, several independent studies have characterized the mutational complement of breast cancer, one of the most common human malignancies (Shah et al., 2009; Stephens et al., 2009; Ding et al., 2010; Banerji et al., 2012; Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012; Shah et al., 2012; Stephens et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Breast cancer is one of the most common human malignancies.
source: For example, several independent studies have characterized the mutational complement of breast cancer, one of the most common human malignancies (Shah et al., 2009; Stephens et al., 2009; Ding et al., 2010; Banerji et al., 2012; Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012; Shah et al., 2012; Stephens et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established epidemiological knowledge.

claim: Most breast cancer resequencing studies report a long tail of rarely mutated genes.
source: Besides confirming previously known cancer genes, such as TP53 and PIK3CA, most studies also report a long tail of rarely mutated genes.
evidence: This is a general observation from cancer genome sequencing studies.

claim: Many mutations in the long tail of rarely mutated genes are likely to be passenger events.
source: While many of these mutations are likely to be passenger events, some of them are potential mediators of tumor phenotypes.
evidence: This is a general principle in cancer genomics.

claim: Some mutations in the long tail of rarely mutated genes are potential mediators of tumor phenotypes.
source: While many of these mutations are likely to be passenger events, some of them are potential mediators of tumor phenotypes.
evidence: This is a general principle in cancer genomics.

claim: Mutations in epigenetic regulators support the stabilization of altered transcriptomic profiles that facilitate the emergence of pro-tumorigenic and metastatic traits.
source: In addition to mutations that directly promote tumorigenesis through specific alterations in cell signaling and repair pathways, many aberrations found in cancers do not affect cell signaling pathways directly, but rather, they support the stabilization of altered transcriptomic profiles that facilitate the emergence of pro-tumorigenic and metastatic traits. Mutations in epigenetic regulators fall into this category (Shen and Laird, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Shen and Laird, 2013.

claim: The phenotypic output of alterations in epigenetic regulators depends on the activity of already existing signaling processes.
source: The phenotypic output of such alterations would depend on the activity of already existing signaling processes.
evidence: This is a logical inference about how epigenetic alterations function.

claim: Examples of epigenetic alterations that result in a phenotypic trait in the presence of a specific transcriptional program have been described.
source: Indeed, examples of epigenetic alterations that result in a phenotypic trait in the presence of a specific transcriptional program have been described (Vanharanta et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Vanharanta et al., 2013.

claim: Aberrations in the multi-step mRNA processing and turnover cascade could lock in aberrant transcriptomic states.
source: Analogously, aberrations in the multi-step mRNA processing and turnover cascade (Moore and Proudfoot, 2009) could also lock in aberrant transcriptomic states.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on analogy with epigenetic alterations, with citation to Moore and Proudfoot, 2009.

claim: Precise regulation of RNA metabolism is fundamental in the generation of biological complexity in both normal and disease states.
source: Precise regulation of RNA metabolism is fundamental in the generation of biological complexity in both normal and disease states (Sharp, 2009; Licatalosi and Darnell, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sharp, 2009 and Licatalosi and Darnell, 2010.

claim: The concerted action of multiple RNA binding proteins regulate the spatial, temporal and functional dynamics of the transcriptome via alternative splicing, alternative polyadenylation and transcript stability.
